title: #58 Use the 4-2 Approach for Independent Work
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton describes a routine for balancing independent practice with paired collaboration: four minutes of silent, independent work followed by two minutes of paired discussion, repeated across a task. He explains the specific timings are deliberate -- four minutes is enough for students to make real progress and generate something worth discussing, without dragging on so long that they get stuck and frustrated, while two minutes is enough for a focused exchange without drifting off-task. He recommends a visible timer to sharpen focus and warns that classes unused to silent work will find the first four minutes feel much longer than it is, so teachers should expect and plan for that adjustment period. For unfamiliar problems specifically, Barton offers a variant, the "30-4-2" approach, which adds an initial 30 seconds where students may not speak or write, echoing his separate tip about silence and no-writing at the start of problem-solving tasks.
points: The 4-2 structure is calibrated, not arbitrary: four minutes is long enough to generate something worth discussing but short enough to avoid frustration; two minutes is long enough for real discussion but short enough to stay on task.
A visible timer is offered as a low-cost lever to sharpen focus during both the silent and paired phases.

Classes unfamiliar with silent independent work will initially experience the four minutes as far longer than it is, so teachers should expect and normalise the adjustment period rather than abandon the routine early.
For unfamiliar problems specifically, Barton layers in a 30-second no-talk, no-write opening (the "30-4-2" variant), linking this tip to his broader thinking on problem-solving routines.
quotes: Well, I have been experimenting with the 4-2 approach for the last few years.
I find 4 minutes is enough time for students to make some progress on their own, so they have work to compare and questions to ask, but not so long that they get stuck and frustrated.
Likewise, 2 minutes is enough for a focussed, productive discussion, but not long enough for those discussions to drift off-task.
If students are not used to working silently, those first 4 minutes will feel more like 4 hours, so feel free to adjust accordingly.

This includes 30 seconds at the start of the task when students are not allowed to speak or write. No speaking allows for a silent, focussed start, and no writing forces students to think hard about the problem instead of diving in with their first instinct.
